ops.title: spctl passing does not mean exec will not hang: quarantine plus a wedged syspolicyd blocks first launch
ops.body:
`spctl -a -vvv -t install <binary>` returning `accepted` / `source=Notarized Developer ID` says the binary **would pass** an assessment you ask for directly. It says nothing about whether `exec` will return.

A binary carrying `com.apple.quarantine` triggers a *synchronous* syspolicyd assessment on first exec, performed by the kernel on your behalf. If syspolicyd is wedged — a known state on this machine, with `sudo killall syspolicyd` as the owner-side fix — that assessment never returns and the process hangs before `main` runs. Meanwhile `spctl` asked directly still answers `accepted`, because it takes a different path.

Measured on cc-patch 0.20.1, back to back on one machine:

```
Caskroom/cc-patch/0.20.0.upgrading/cc-patch --version   exit=0    out=0.20.0
Caskroom/cc-patch/0.20.1/cc-patch --version             exit=124  (4 attempts)
spctl -a -vvv -t install .../0.20.1/cc-patch            accepted, Notarized Developer ID
xattr -d com.apple.quarantine .../0.20.1/cc-patch
Caskroom/cc-patch/0.20.1/cc-patch --version             exit=0    out=0.20.1
```

I used the `spctl` pass to rule out Gatekeeper and concluded the released artifact was a bad build. It was not; it was quarantined. The `go build`-from-source control I ran alongside pointed the same wrong way, because a locally built binary is never quarantined — so it isolated "downloaded vs built", not "bad vs good".

**How to apply.** When a freshly downloaded macOS binary hangs with no output, check `xattr -l` **before** reaching for `spctl`, `codesign` or a source build. An empty `xattr` on a working copy beside a `com.apple.quarantine` on the hanging one is the whole diagnosis. Treat `spctl` as answering a different question than the one you have. A long-stuck invocation of the same binary elsewhere on the machine is corroboration, not a separate bug.
